caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:pag-2
attempts.entry_title: Early adolescent adversity and vlPAG/DR threat responding (Moaddab, Wright and McDannald 2020)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up, one did not, and the weight-gain result could not be tested. EAA rats had more cue-responsive vlPAG neurons (133/203 against 80/151), inflated cue responses, and stronger fear output signaling in cue-inhibited neurons. Reduced threat probability signaling and decoupled firing in cue-excited neurons held only in part, the first at p = 0.055 and the second only with the authors' script normalization. The link between firing and fear output in cue-inhibited neurons did not reproduce, likely because the paper's figure used a different cue window than its legend gives. Body weights and pre-surgery learning sessions are absent from the dataset, and the behavioral and baseline controls held.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Moaddab, Wright and McDannald (2020) on CRCNS data set pag-2, which holds 354 single units recorded in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray and dorsal raphe of 8 Control and 12 early adolescent adversity rats during fear discrimination, with the authors' cube and analysis script. It tests the behaviour during recording, the selection of cue-excited and cue-inhibited neurons, their normalized firing, the single-unit regressions on fear output and threat probability, and the firing and signaling relationships. The body weights and pre-surgery sessions of Figure 1 are not in the data set.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Moaddab et al. (2020) from CRCNS pag-2

outcomes.statement: Early adolescent adversity slowed body weight gain. Body weight showed a group by day interaction, and Control rats gained more weight from P24 to P35 (P35/P24) than EAA rats; weights were equivalent before adversity and in adulthood.
outcomes.source: Results, first paragraph (before the heading Higher proportion of EAA cue-responsive neurons); Figure 1B and 1C
outcomes.quote: Body weights were equivalent prior to adversity, weight gain slowed in EAA rats, but body weights were equivalent between groups in adulthood. ... found a significant group × day interaction (F 13,234 = 4.20, p = 3.00 × 10 –6 ... Independent samples t test for body weight change found a significant difference between groups (t 18 = 6.11, p = 9.00 × 10 –6

statistics.about: body weight, group by day interaction, 14 days from P24 to P55
body weight change P35/P24, Con against EAA

outcomes.notes: The data set holds no body weights. Its data.zip contains the 354 unit files of the recording sessions, the authors' cube built from them, the script vlpagAnalysis.m and three cue sounds, and the data description lists nothing else. The paper names no other deposit.

outcomes.statement: Both groups acquired fear discrimination over the eight pre-surgery sessions (danger > uncertainty > safety). EAA rats acquired it faster, giving a group by cue by session interaction, but in the final session there was a main effect of cue and no group by cue interaction.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3 (Control and EAA rats acquired discrimination); Figure 1E and 1F
outcomes.quote: EAA rats acquired discrimination faster than Controls, but discrimination levels were equivalent between groups by the final discrimination session ... found a group × cue × session interaction (F 14,252 = 1.99, p = 0.02 ... ANOVA restricted to the final discrimination session found a main effect of cue (F 2,36 = 151.45, p = 2.97 × 10 –18 ... but no group × cue interaction (F 2,36 = 1.55, p = 0.23

statistics.about: group by cue by session, sessions 1 to 8
statistics.test: ANOVA, repeated measures on session, factors group and cue

statistics.about: final session, main effect of cue

outcomes.notes: The eight pre-surgery discrimination sessions are not in the data set, which holds only the recording sessions (each unit file is one recording session with spikes), and are not deposited elsewhere as far as the paper and the data description say.

outcomes.statement: Control and EAA rats had equivalent baseline nose poke rates during recording sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, Higher proportion of EAA cue-responsive neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: Control and EAA rats showed equivalent baseline nose poke rates (t 18 = 1.24, p = 0.23
outcomes.notes: Baseline poke rate in the 20 s before cue onset, one value per rat over its recording sessions (each session counted once). Control 23.08 and EAA 19.22 pokes per minute, t(18) = 1.19, p = 0.25 (the paper t = 1.24, p = 0.23). Both readings (mean of session means, trials pooled) give the same values, as every session has 32 trials.

outcomes.statement: During recording sessions both groups showed high fear to danger, less to uncertainty and least to safety, with a main effect of cue, no group by cue interaction, and each cue pair differing in each group.
outcomes.source: Results, Higher proportion of EAA cue-responsive neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: ANOVA for mean suppression ratios [factors ... found a main effect of cue (F 2,36 = 199.47, p = 3.33 × 10 –20 ... but no group × cue interaction (F 2,36 = 0.24, p = 0.79 ... Paired samples t tests confirmed differing ratios for each group and cue (danger vs. uncertainty; uncertainty vs. safety; all t > 3.00, all p ≤ 0.01)

statistics.about: danger against uncertainty and uncertainty against safety, each group

outcomes.notes: Under all six readings (session means or trials pooled; 0/0 trials set to 0, dropped or set to 1) the cue effect is F(2,36) = 179.5 to 194.5, p <= 1.9e-19, the group by cue interaction p = 0.84 to 0.90, and all four paired tests have p <= 0.0091 with danger > uncertainty > safety. Mean ratios (0/0 as 0, session means) Control 0.919, 0.715, 0.117 and EAA 0.900, 0.690, 0.049.
deviations: Sessions are counted once per rat, although several units share each session.
A third treatment of trials without pokes (ratio set to 1) is added to the claims file's two, because the authors' cube stores 1 for them (cer.cue).

outcomes.statement: 32 of 151 Control neurons (21.2%) and 49 of 203 EAA neurons (24.1%) were cue-excited; 48 of 151 Control neurons (31.8%) and 84 of 203 EAA neurons (41.4%) were cue-inhibited.
outcomes.source: Results, Higher proportion of EAA cue-responsive neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: We identified 32/151 Control neurons (21.2%) and 49/203 EAA neurons (24.1%) that were cue-excited ... We identified 48/151 Control neurons (31.8%) and 84/203 EAA neurons (41.4%) that were cue-inhibited
outcomes.notes: With the raw rates stored in the authors' cube and reading (b) (excitation over first 1 s and last 5 s, inhibition over first 5 s and last 5 s), the counts are the paper's exactly. With exact rates from the spike times, reading (c) is within tolerance (30, 48, 51, 89) and reading (b) gives 30, 50, 54, 87, the Control inhibited count outside the tolerance. Reading (a) is outside under both rate sources. The selection used by the dependent claims is (b) with the cube's rates; with exact rates 14 of 354 units change class.
deviations: The cube stores the raw rates truncated to whole Hz (uint8). The authors' script runs the selection t tests on these stored rates (vlpagAnalysis.m, lines 9 to 67) with reading (b) (lines 136 to 147 and 225 to 236); this attempt follows the script for the rates, as the Methods say only raw firing rate (Hz), and shows the exact rates as a variant.

outcomes.statement: A higher proportion of EAA neurons than Control neurons were cue-responsive (133/203, 65.5%, against 80/151, 53.0%).
outcomes.source: Results, Higher proportion of EAA cue-responsive neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: Combining the cue-excited and cue-inhibited populations in each group revealed a higher proportion of EAA cue-responsive neurons (133/203, 65.5%) compared to Controls (80/151, 53.0%); χ 2 = 5.68, p = 0.02
outcomes.notes: 133/203 against 80/151, chi-square = 5.68, p = 0.017 without continuity correction (the paper 5.68, p = 0.02). With exact rates (b) 0.675 and 0.556, chi-square = 5.19, p = 0.023. Every reading and rate source gives EAA higher with p < 0.05 (p = 0.004 to 0.030).

outcomes.statement: Baseline firing rates did not differ between Control and EAA neurons of any functional type, while across groups baseline firing differed by functional type and was lowest for cue-excited neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Higher proportion of EAA cue-responsive neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 2E and 2F
outcomes.quote: Independent samples t tests found no differences in baseline firing between Control and EAA cue-excited, cue-inhibited and neurons outside the selection criteria (all t < 1.10, all p > 0.25). By contrast, one-way ANOVA for the three functional neuron types, collapsing across Control and EAA groups found a main effect of functional type (F 2,346 = 7.35, p = 0.001). Baseline firing rates were lowest for cue-excited neurons.

statistics.about: Con against EAA, each functional type

outcomes.notes: With the selection used here, the group t tests have p = 0.26 to 0.96 (all |t| < 1.13) under both baseline windows, the type effect F(2,351) = 6.44, p = 0.0018 (10 s) and 6.78, p = 0.0013 (2 s), and cue-excited neurons have the lowest mean (13.9 Hz against 22.0 and 25.3). With the exact-rate selection the smallest group p is 0.12 and the type effect p = 0.0001 to 0.0002. The paper's error df is 346 against 351 here.
deviations: The ANOVA uses all 354 neurons (df 351); the paper's df of 346 implies five fewer, which are not named.

outcomes.statement: Control and EAA cue-excited neurons differed in the temporal pattern of their cue-selective firing, a group by cue by bin interaction that held with bregma recording level as a factor.
outcomes.source: Results, Inflated cue responses in EAA neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 4A and 4B
outcomes.quote: Critically, the temporal pattern of selective firing differed for Control and EAA cue-excited neurons. ... revealed a group × cue × bin interaction (F 110,8360 = 3.32, p = 3.13 × 10 –28 ... The interaction held when bregma recording level was included as an ANOVA factor (F 110,8360 = 1.49, p = 0.001

statistics.test: ANOVA, factors group, cue and bin

statistics.about: group by cue by bin, with bregma level as a factor

outcomes.notes: Group by cue by bin interaction F(110,8690) = 1.30, p = 0.019 (the paper F(110,8360) = 3.32, p = 3e-28). With the script's normalization F = 1.40, p = 0.004; with the exact-rate selection F = 1.29, p = 0.021. The part with bregma level as a factor could not be run, as the data set gives no bregma level per rat (only the number of rats at each of four levels), and the authors' script does not mention bregma. The outcome is partial because only the first part of the criterion could be tested; it held.
deviations: The ANOVA with bregma level was not run (no bregma level per rat in the data set or the authors' script).
Uncorrected type III mixed ANOVA on all 81 neurons; the paper's error df implies 78.

outcomes.statement: In the first 1 s of the cue, EAA cue-excited neurons fired more than Control neurons (main effect of group), with a significant group difference to safety; both groups still discriminated danger from uncertainty and uncertainty from safety.
outcomes.source: Results, Inflated cue responses in EAA neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: ANOVA for the first 1 s cue interval revealed a main effect of group (F 1,79 = 4.96, p = 0.03 ... Compared to Controls, EAA neurons showed excessive firing to safety (Bonferroni-corrected, independent samples t test, t 79 = 3.61, p = 0.001; Fig. 4 C). Yet in the first 1 s of cue presentation, Control and EAA cue-excited neurons each showed cellular discrimination between danger and uncertainty (Bonferroni-corrected, paired samples t test, all t > 2.50, all p < 0.025), as well as uncertainty and safety (all t > 3.00, all p < 0.025)
outcomes.notes: Group F(1,79) = 5.19, p = 0.025, EAA higher; safety t(79) = -3.46, p = 0.0009; paired danger against uncertainty Control p = 0.0047, EAA p = 0.023, uncertainty against safety p <= 0.0018 in both. With the script's normalization the statistics are the paper's (group F = 4.96, p = 0.029; safety t = -3.60, p = 0.0005 against 3.61, 0.001), and the exact-rate selection also meets every part.

outcomes.statement: Control and EAA cue-inhibited neurons differed in the temporal pattern of their cue firing (a group by cue by bin interaction that held with bregma level as a factor). Control neurons decreased firing equally to danger and uncertainty with little change to safety, sustained over the cue; EAA neurons decreased most to danger, less to uncertainty, mostly in the first half of the cue.
outcomes.source: Results, Inflated cue responses in EAA neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4D and 4E
outcomes.quote: EAA cue-inhibited neurons showed enhanced decreases in firing to danger, lesser decreases in firing to uncertainty and little change to safety ... revealed a group × cue × bin interaction (F 110,14190 = 1.69, p = 9.00 × 10 –6 ... The interaction was observed when bregma recording level was included as an ANOVA factor (F 110,13970 = 1.34, p = 0.01

statistics.test: ANOVA, factors group, cue and bin

statistics.about: group by cue by bin, with bregma level as a factor

outcomes.notes: Group by cue by bin interaction F(110,14300) = 1.54, p = 0.00024 (the paper F(110,14190) = 1.69, p = 9e-6); script normalization p = 4.4e-6, exact-rate selection p = 2.5e-5. The means follow the described pattern (Control danger and uncertainty -0.75 and -0.61 in the first half, -0.69 and -0.67 in the second, safety near 0; EAA danger -1.06 and uncertainty -0.79 in the first half, -0.74 and -0.76 in the second). The bregma part could not be tested (no bregma level per rat in the data set or the authors' script); the outcome is partial for that reason only.
deviations: The ANOVA with bregma level was not run (no bregma level per rat in the data set or the authors' script).

outcomes.statement: In the first 5 s of the cue, EAA cue-inhibited neurons decreased firing more than Control neurons (main effect of group), with a greater decrease to danger; the group difference to uncertainty fell short of the corrected level.
outcomes.source: Results, Inflated cue responses in EAA neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4F
outcomes.quote: EAA cue-inhibited neurons also showed greater decreases in firing to danger compared to Control neurons (Bonferroni-corrected, independent samples t test, t 130 = 2.70, p = 0.008; Fig. 4 F). The group difference in firing to uncertainty fell short of the Bonferroni-corrected p value (t 130 = 2.38, p = 0.019). Finally, ANOVA for mean firing over the first 5 s of cue presentation revealed a main effect of group (F 1,130 = 10.82, p = 0.001

statistics.about: main effect of group, first 5 s

outcomes.notes: First 5 s, group F(1,130) = 9.15, p = 0.003, EAA lower; danger t(130) = 2.58, p = 0.011, EAA lower; uncertainty t(130) = 1.76, p = 0.080. The script's normalization gives the paper's values (F = 10.81, danger t = 2.69, p = 0.008, uncertainty t = 2.39, p = 0.0185); the exact-rate selection also meets the criterion (F = 13.08, danger p = 0.002).

outcomes.statement: In the first half of the cue, EAA cue-inhibited neurons discriminated danger from uncertainty, while Control cue-inhibited neurons did not.
outcomes.source: Results, Inflated cue responses in EAA neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4D to 4F
outcomes.quote: Supporting an interaction, EAA cue-inhibited neurons (Bonferroni-corrected, paired samples t test, t 83 = 3.14, p = 0.002), but not Control cue-inhibited neurons (t 47 = 1.40, p = 0.17), showed cellular discrimination between danger and uncertainty in the first half of cue presentation.
outcomes.notes: EAA danger -1.056 against uncertainty -0.791, t(83) = -3.21, p = 0.0019, below 0.025 and 0.0167; Control -0.749 against -0.614, t(47) = -1.29, p = 0.20. Script normalization EAA t = -3.14, p = 0.0024 and Control t = -1.40, p = 0.17 (the paper 3.14, 0.002 and 1.40, 0.17).

outcomes.statement: Control cue-excited neurons signaled threat probability (positive betas from cue onset, rising over the cue) with fear output betas near zero; EAA cue-excited neurons showed lower threat probability betas and similar fear output betas, a group by regressor interaction.
outcomes.source: Results, Diminished threat probability signaling in EAA cue-excited neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 5A to 5C
outcomes.quote: EAA cue-excited neurons showed diminished threat probability signaling (Fig. 5 B). ... revealed a group × regressor interaction (F 1,65 = 6.80, p = 0.01 ... The mean beta coefficient for the entirety of cue presentation differed for threat probability (independent samples t test, t 66 = 2.71, p = 0.01), but not fear output (t 66 = 0.17, p = 0.86), between Control and EAA cue-excited neurons

statistics.test: ANOVA, repeated measures on 1 s interval (10), factors group and regressor

statistics.about: threat probability beta, whole cue, Con against EAA
fear output beta, whole cue, Con against EAA

outcomes.notes: Under the adopted reading (the cube's trial-wise Z score, 0/0 trials set to 1, as the authors' script regresses them) the whole-cue threat probability beta is higher in Control (0.953 against 0.558, t(79) = 2.12, p = 0.037), the fear output betas do not differ (p = 0.87), but the group by regressor interaction is F(1,79) = 3.79, p = 0.055. Of the claims file's six readings none meets all three parts; (b) with 0/0 trials dropped gives the same partial pattern (interaction p = 0.055, threat p = 0.047). The cube's Z score with 0/0 trials set to 0 meets all three (interaction p = 0.031, threat p = 0.044), but it is not the adopted combination and is further from the paper's statistics. The claims file's own rule (one of its six readings) gives the same outcome, partial, so the outcome does not rest on the adopted reading. Control threat betas are positive from the first interval and rise (0.72 to 1.22). With the exact-rate selection no reading meets the threat probability part (smallest p = 0.060). The paper's F(1,65) and t(66) imply about 67 of the 81 neurons. The question of which trial-wise firing and which 0/0 treatment the paper used is for its authors (see findings).
deviations: Reading adopted for every regression claim. The trial-wise normalized firing and the treatment of trials without pokes are open in the paper (Results, Diminished threat probability signaling, paragraph 1, says only "normalized firing rate for each trial ... in 1 s bins"). The authors' script in the data set regresses vlPAGcube.fire.z.s1.interval (each trial's own 2 s baseline subtracted, Z scored over all trials and bins) on vlPAGcube.cer.cue (which stores 1 for 0/0 trials) (vlpagAnalysis.m, lines 2162 to 2171, printed in the notebook's data check). That combination is adopted for every regression claim (Figs. 5, S4, 6, S5, 7, S6), the same for each, and the twelve combinations of the claims file's readings and the script's are all shown. Here the claims file's readings give the same outcome. Of the twelve it gives the paper's printed statistics for Figs. 5A to G and 6 most closely (mean relative deviation 0.076, next 0.167, the claims file's six readings 0.236 to 0.724).

The tests use all 81 cue-excited neurons (df 79); the paper's df implies about 67. Trials without pokes, missing betas and rank-deficient designs do not explain the difference (24 of the 81 come from sessions with a 0/0 trial, no beta is missing, every design is of full rank), and the script has no exclusion step.

outcomes.statement: The threat tuning curve of cue-excited neurons peaked at an uncertainty assignment of 0.500 in both groups; the EAA curve had the same shape but was lower across all assignments (main effect of assignment and of group, no interaction).
outcomes.source: Results, Diminished threat probability signaling in EAA cue-excited neurons, paragraphs 3 and 4; Figure 5D
outcomes.quote: The tuning curve for EAA cue-excited neurons was identical in shape, but was diminished across all assignments. ... revealed a main effect of assignment (F 8,624 = 18.88, p = 1.71 × 10 –25 ... but most critically a main effect of group (F 1,78 = 4.01, p = 0.049 ... and no group × assignment interaction (F 8,624 = 1.25, p = 0.27

statistics.test: ANOVA, repeated measures on assignment (9), factor group

outcomes.notes: Under the adopted reading both curves peak at 0.500, assignment F(8,632) = 18.69, p = 2.8e-25, group F(1,79) = 4.15, p = 0.045 with EAA lower (0.34 to 0.60 against 0.56 to 1.00), no interaction (p = 0.22). Peaks are at 0.500 under ten of twelve readings (EAA 0.625 under b with 0/0 dropped or set to 1) and the assignment effect holds under all; the group effect has p < 0.05 only with the cube's Z score and 0/0 trials dropped or set to 1 (p = 0.046, 0.045). Under the claims file's readings (a to c) the group effect has p = 0.07 to 0.24 and the claim is not reproduced, so the outcome rests on the assumption. The adopted combination is the script's and the one whose statistics are closest to the paper's (assignment and group F 18.69 and 4.15 against 18.88 and 4.01; interaction F 1.34 against 1.25).
deviations: Assumption. The reading adopted for fig5abc-excited-reduced-threat-probability, the cube's fire.z.s1 regressed on cer.cue as the script does (vlpagAnalysis.m lines 2162 to 2171, printed in the notebook's data check). Here the claims file's readings give a different outcome.

outcomes.statement: Using the peak uncertainty assignment (0.500) in place of the actual probability gave the same pattern of threat probability signaling in cue-excited neurons and of fear output signaling in cue-inhibited neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Diminished threat probability signaling, paragraph 4, and Enhanced fear output signaling, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure S4 (not in the text supplied)
outcomes.quote: Importantly, using the peak uncertainty assignment for linear regression returned an identical pattern of threat probability signaling as did the actual uncertainty assignment
outcomes.notes: Under the adopted reading the cue-excited whole-cue threat difference is significant with 0.375 (p = 0.037) and 0.5 (p = 0.040), Control higher, and the cue-inhibited last-5 s fear output difference with 0.375 (p = 0.021) and 0.5 (p = 0.011), EAA more negative. Under nine of the twelve readings significance and direction are the same with both values; under b with 0/0 dropped or set to 1 and the cube's Z score with 0/0 set to 0, one test changes side of 0.05. Readings (a) and (c) of the claims file give the same significance and direction with both values, so the outcome does not rest on the adopted reading; under (a) to (c) the cue-excited threat difference is not significant with either value (p = 0.091 to 0.265). With Matlab's solution for the one cue-inhibited design not of full rank, the cue-inhibited test has p = 0.023 and 0.012.
deviations: The supplement was not available; the comparison is the one the criterion names. Judged under the reading adopted for fig5abc-excited-reduced-threat-probability; the claims file's readings (a) and (c) give the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: Control cue-inhibited neurons signaled a mix of threat probability and fear output (negative betas for both). In EAA cue-inhibited neurons the signals diverged in the second half of the cue, fear output persisting and threat probability diminishing (group by regressor by interval interaction); fear output betas in the last 5 s were more negative in EAA, threat probability betas did not differ.
outcomes.source: Results, Enhanced fear output signaling in EAA cue-inhibited neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 5E to 5G
outcomes.quote: Signals diverged thereafter, with fear output persisting and threat probability diminishing (Fig. 5 F). ... revealed a group × regressor × interval interaction (F 9,1170 = 2.14, p = 0.02 ... Mean beta coefficient for fear output was more negative in EAA cue-inhibited neurons compared to Control neurons for the last half of cue presentation (independent samples t test, t 130 = 2.31, p = 0.02; Fig. 5 G). Beta coefficients for threat probability in the same period did not differ (t 130 = 0.81, p = 0.42).

statistics.test: ANOVA, repeated measures on 1 s interval (10), factors group and regressor

statistics.about: fear output beta, last 5 s, Con against EAA
threat probability beta, last 5 s, Con against EAA

outcomes.notes: Under the adopted reading the group by regressor by interval interaction is F(9,1170) = 2.15, p = 0.023, the last-5 s fear output beta is -0.386 in EAA against -0.220 in Control (t = 2.34, p = 0.021) and the threat betas do not differ (p = 0.41). Readings (a) and (c) of the claims file meet all three parts under every 0/0 treatment, so the outcome does not rest on the assumption; (b) misses the fear output part (p = 0.054 to 0.13). The adopted reading's statistics are close to the paper's (F = 2.15, t = 2.34 and 0.82 against 2.14, 2.31 and 0.81). With the exact-rate selection the interaction is not significant under any reading (p = 0.060 to 0.19). With Matlab's solution for the one design not of full rank, F = 2.14, p = 0.024 and the fear output t = 2.30, p = 0.023 (threat p = 0.41).
deviations: One cue-inhibited neuron (mh38101617epr38bSPK05a, EAA) comes from a session with no poke during any cue, so with 0/0 trials set to 1 or dropped its suppression ratio equals the constant. The regressions give it minimum-norm betas (numpy lstsq), where Matlab regress, which the script uses, sets its fear output beta to 0. Matlab's solution is run as a variant for the adopted reading; no outcome changes. This applies to every claim on cue-inhibited betas (Figs. 5E to G, S4, 7, S6).

outcomes.statement: In Control cue-excited neurons, danger and uncertainty firing in the first 1 s of the cue predicted the whole-cue threat probability beta; in EAA cue-excited neurons they did not, and the relationships differed between groups. Safety firing was unrelated in both groups, and that relationship did not differ between groups.
outcomes.source: Results, Cue firing and threat probability signaling decoupled in EAA cue-excited neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 6A to 6F
outcomes.quote: Danger firing and threat probability signaling were coupled in Control cue-excited neurons ... (R 2 = 0.56, p = 7.54 × 10 –7 ; Fig. 6 A). ... (R 2 = 0.01, p = 0.61; Fig. 6 B). Importantly, the relationship between danger firing and threat probability signaling significantly differed between Control and EAA cue-excited neurons (Fisher r-to-z transformation, Z = 3.80, p = 0.0001). ... Control cue-excited neurons showed a positive relationship (R 2 = 0.22, p = 0.007; Fig. 6 C), EAA cue-excited neurons showed zero relationship (R 2 = 0.05, p = 0.14; Fig. 6 D) and these relationships significantly differed (Fisher r-to-z transformation, Z = 3.05, p = 0.0011). Safety firing and threat probability signaling were not related in either population
outcomes.notes: Firing normalized as the claims file fixes it (Methods). The danger part holds under all twelve regression readings (adopted Control r = 0.51, p = 0.003; EAA r = -0.00, p = 0.98; Z = 2.37, one-tailed p = 0.009). The uncertainty part fails under all twelve, as the Control correlation is not significant (adopted r = 0.09, p = 0.62), and EAA safety firing correlates negatively with the beta (p = 0.0084 to 0.040 over the twelve readings; adopted p = 0.040). With the script's normalization of the firing, run as a full variant under all twelve regression readings, every part holds under nine of them (all but those with firing b), and under the adopted one the statistics are the paper's (Control danger R2 = 0.566, p = 6.8e-7; uncertainty R2 = 0.218, p = 0.007; Z = 3.83 and 3.07, one-tailed p = 6e-5 and 0.0011). Under the Methods' normalization the safety part also fails under all twelve. The verifier would give reproduced on the script's normalization; the outcome is kept, as recorded under verifications.
deviations: The Methods' normalization (claims file) and the script's normalization give different outcomes. The Methods say "Mean differential firing was Z score normalized across all trial types" after averaging the trials (Methods, Z score normalization), the claims file follows them, and where the Methods and the code disagree the Methods decide (reader, step 2); the script's result is shown as a full variant.

outcomes.statement: In cue-excited neurons, cue firing did not predict fear output signaling for any cue in either group, and the relationships did not differ between groups.
outcomes.source: Results, Cue firing and threat probability signaling decoupled, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure S5 (not in the text supplied)
outcomes.quote: An identical analysis comparing firing to fear output signaling found no predictive relationships for any cues, and no differences between these relationships for Control and EAA cue-excited neurons
outcomes.notes: Under all twelve readings none of the six correlations and none of the three comparisons has p < 0.05 (adopted reading, smallest correlation p = 0.23, smallest one-tailed comparison p = 0.13). With the script's normalization the adopted reading also has none (smallest one-tailed comparison p = 0.059), but six of the twelve readings have one comparison with one-tailed p < 0.05 (smallest 0.010).

outcomes.statement: In cue-inhibited neurons, last-5 s danger firing did not predict the last-5 s fear output beta in either group; uncertainty firing predicted it positively in EAA but not in Control neurons, and safety firing predicted it negatively in both groups; none of these relationships differed between groups.
outcomes.source: Results, Cue firing and fear output signaling coupled in EAA cue-inhibited neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 7A to 7F
outcomes.quote: Degree of danger firing failed to predict fear output signaling in either population (Control ... R 2 = 0.004, p = 0.67; EAA ... R 2 = 0.02, p = 0.24; Fig. 7 A, B) and these relationships did not differ (Fisher r-to-z transformation, Z = 1.04, p = 0.15). EAA cue-inhibited neurons, but not Control, showed a positive predictive relationship between uncertainty firing and fear output (Control ... R 2 = 0.04, p = 0.16; EAA ... R 2 = 0. 20, p = 2.59 × 10 –5 ... but these relationships did not differ between groups (Fisher r-to-z transformation, Z = 1.43, p = 0.08). Equivalent negative predictive relationships between safety firing and fear output signaling were also found in both groups (Fisher r-to-z transformation, Z = 0.60, p = 0.54).
outcomes.notes: Under every reading the Control uncertainty firing correlates positively and significantly with the last-5 s fear output beta (Methods' normalization r = 0.35 to 0.73, p <= 0.015, weakest under firing c; adopted r = 0.71, p = 1.2e-8; the paper R2 = 0.04, p = 0.16), so the uncertainty part fails, and with it the condition for a partial outcome. Under the adopted reading the danger correlations have p = 0.054 and 0.15, both safety correlations are negative with p = 0.026 and 0.004, and the uncertainty comparison is Z = 2.06, one-tailed p = 0.020. The script's normalization, run under all twelve readings, also fails the uncertainty part in each (adopted Control uncertainty R2 = 0.49, p = 2.8e-8). With firing over the first 5 s of the cue, the only window besides the whole cue that the script computes for cue-inhibited neurons (vlpagAnalysis.m lines 2796 to 2817, printed in the notebook), every part holds under the adopted reading with both normalizations, and with the script's normalization the statistics are the paper's (Control uncertainty R2 = 0.042, p = 0.16 against 0.04, 0.16; safety Control R2 = 0.14, p = 0.009 and EAA 0.218, p = 7.7e-6 against 0.14, 0.009 and 0.22, 8.9e-6; safety Z = 0.60 against 0.60). Under all twelve regression readings, first-5 s firing meets every part with firing (b) or (d) (all six with the script's normalization, five of six with the Methods'), the Control uncertainty correlation stays significant with (a) (p <= 0.004), and the danger and safety parts fail with (c). With Matlab's solution for the one design not of full rank the parts that hold are the same. The paper's Fig. 7 was evidently computed on first-5 s firing, while its legend and Results say the last 5 s; the claims file follows the legend, so the outcome stays.

outcomes.statement: In cue-inhibited neurons, cue firing also predicted threat probability signaling in both groups, with no difference between Control and EAA for any relationship.
outcomes.source: Results, Cue firing and fear output signaling coupled in EAA cue-inhibited neurons, paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure S6 (not in the text supplied)
outcomes.quote: Cue firing was also predictive of threat probability signaling in both groups (see Supplementary Fig. S6 online), but there were no differences between Control and EAA cue-inhibited neurons for any predictive relationship.
outcomes.notes: Under every reading danger firing predicts the last-5 s threat beta in both groups (adopted r = 0.73 and 0.84). No comparison has p < 0.05 two-tailed under any reading; one-tailed the danger comparison has p = 0.036 and 0.038 with the cube's Z score and 0/0 trials set to 0 or dropped, and p = 0.052 under the adopted reading. Under readings (a) to (c) no comparison has one-tailed p < 0.10. With the script's normalization every part holds under all twelve readings (smallest one-tailed comparison p = 0.096).
deviations: The criterion shows both tails; the outcome is judged with both under the adopted reading, where they agree.
The design not of full rank described under fig5efg-inhibited-fear-output; with Matlab's solution every part still holds (smallest one-tailed comparison p = 0.052).

findings.statement: The units come from 182 recording sessions (74 Control, 108 EAA), each with its own trial table, where the paper and the data description state 72 Control and 107 EAA sessions. The unit counts (151 and 203) and rat counts (8 and 12) match. No session holds more than one behaviour program and no two sessions share a trial table, so the extra sessions are not duplicates.
The group of each rat (Control or EAA) is given only by lists in the authors' script vlpagAnalysis.m (lines 99 to 122), not by the data description or the files.

The event codes EVT01 to EVT14 of the unit files are not described. EVT09, EVT11 and EVT12 are the cue onsets, but which is danger, uncertainty or safety depends on the behaviour program in the file name (epr38a, b, c); EVT08 holds the shocks, EVT13 the nose pokes, EVT14 a marker about 31.5 s after each onset, and EVT02 could not be identified.

The data description says poke.base is the baseline nose poke rate 2 s prior to cue presentation. It is the rate in the 20 s before cue onset (99.8% of trials; 4.2% match a 2 s window), in pokes per minute, a unit the description does not give.
The data description gives the uncertainty shock rows a shock probability of 0.25; the paper and the description's own summary give 0.375.
No bregma recording level per rat is given; the description gives only how many rats were at each of four levels, so the paper's ANOVAs with bregma level cannot be repeated.
The body weights (Fig. 1B, C) and the eight pre-surgery discrimination sessions (Fig. 1E, F) are not in the data set.

The cube stores raw firing rates as unsigned integers truncated towards zero, so units firing below 1 Hz have stored rates of 0 (775 trials with spikes have a stored 10 s baseline of 0). The paper's counts of cue-excited and cue-inhibited neurons follow exactly from these truncated rates; with exact rates from the spike times the Control cue-inhibited count is 54, not 48.

Spikes and nose pokes are stored only around the trials, from about 20 s before to about 33.5 s after each cue onset (99.98% of spikes and 99.99% of nose pokes fall within 20.5 s before to 33.5 s after an onset), not over the whole session, which the data description does not say.

The cube stores a suppression ratio of 1 for the 255 unit-trials (143 session-trials) with no nose poke in the baseline or the cue, where the ratio is 0/0; the paper does not say how such trials are treated.

The Methods describe the normalized firing as the trial-averaged differential firing Z scored over all bins and trial types of a neuron. The authors' script instead averages the cube's trial-wise Z scores (each trial's own 2 s baseline subtracted, Z scored over all trials and bins). With the script's version the statistics of Figs. 4C, 4F and 6 are the paper's to the second digit (for example group F(1,79) = 4.96 and F(1,130) = 10.81 against 4.96 and 10.82; Fig. 6 Control danger R2 = 0.566 against 0.56); with the Methods' version they differ, and the uncertainty part of Fig. 6 fails.

Question for the paper's authors. Which trial-wise normalized firing entered the single-unit regressions (Figs. 5 to 7), and how were trials with no nose poke in baseline and cue treated? This attempt assumed the cube's fire.z.s1 regressed on cer.cue (0/0 stored as 1), as vlpagAnalysis.m does; the claims file's readings (trial firing minus the cue's mean or the trial's own 2 s baseline Z scored with the neuron's normalization, or raw firing Z scored over all trials) give a non-significant group effect for Fig. 5D (p = 0.07 to 0.24) where the adopted reading gives p = 0.045.

Question for the paper's authors. Several reported error degrees of freedom are smaller than the selected neurons give (Fig. 5A to C t(66) and F(1,65) for 81 cue-excited neurons; Fig. 4A, B F(110,8360); Fig. 2E, F F(2,346) for 354 neurons). Which neurons were left out of these tests, and why? Trials without pokes, missing betas and rank-deficient designs do not account for it, and the script has no exclusion step.

The legend of Fig. 7 and the Results say cue-inhibited firing was taken over the last 5 s of the cue. The authors' script computes per-neuron cue-inhibited firing only over the first 5 s and the whole cue (vlpagAnalysis.m lines 2796 to 2817), and the paper's Fig. 7 statistics follow from the first 5 s (with the script's normalization and regression, Control uncertainty R2 = 0.042, p = 0.16 against 0.04, 0.16; safety Z = 0.60 against 0.60). With last-5 s firing, Control uncertainty firing correlates with the fear output beta at R2 = 0.49 (p = 2.8e-8).
Question for the paper's authors. Was the firing in Fig. 7 taken over the first 5 s of the cue, as the statistics this attempt obtains suggest, and not the last 5 s the legend gives?

verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier checked the archive's file list, tested mixed_anova and fisher_r_to_z on synthetic data and checked the windows. Its report gave its own outcome for each claim; 19 of 20 agree with the record, and it disagrees on fig6-excited-firing-threat-decoupled.

disagreements.reason: Reproduced only under the script's normalization (NFc) with (d, one) betas, where Control danger R2 = 0.566, uncertainty R2 = 0.218, Z = 3.83 and 3.07 and all parts pass. NFc reproduces the paper almost digit for digit (Figs. 4C, 4F, 6), so it is evidently what the authors computed, and the Methods wording ("Z score normalized across all trial types") also allows the SD to be taken over trial-level bins. NFc was run for the correlations only with (d, one) betas and should have been a full reading. The claims file's opening comment lists only the Methods' normalization, a gap in the claims file, not a misreading of the text (B1).

The verifier agreed with all 20 outcomes and listed sentences the outputs do not support and points that remain. One point is not tied to a claim, the stated storage windows of spikes and nose pokes (cell 7 and the finding); the data check now prints the extents of both, and the text and the finding give about 20 s before to about 33.5 s after each onset.

entries.name: moaddab-2020
entries.title: Early adolescent adversity and vlPAG/DR threat responding (Moaddab, Wright and McDannald 2020)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Moaddab, Wright and McDannald (2020) on CRCNS data set pag-2, which holds 354 single units recorded in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray and dorsal raphe of 8 Control and 12 early adolescent adversity rats during fear discrimination, with the authors' cube and analysis script. It tests the behaviour during recording, the selection of cue-excited and cue-inhibited neurons, their normalized firing, the single-unit regressions on fear output and threat probability, and the firing and signaling relationships. The body weights and pre-surgery sessions of Figure 1 are not in the data set.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Moaddab et al. (2020) from CRCNS pag-2
